reason: The run is almost uniform on "hand over", including for Judas, where the tradition says "betray". That is a deliberate departure which each chapter reached independently, so it should be fixed in the register. The run also splits on the same sense in three places: "committed to the grace of God" (Acts 14:26) against "entrusted to the grace of the Lord" (Acts 15:40); "handed over for our trespasses" (Rom 4:25) against "gave him up" and "gave himself up" (Rom 8:32, Gal 2:20, Eph 5:2, 5:25); and "handed on" against "handed down" for passing on teaching.
sense: To transfer a person or thing into another's custody, power or control. This is the main sense and covers Judas, the authorities, Pilate, God, and the handing over of property or authority.

alternates.when: A teacher or messenger passes teaching, tradition or instructions directly to his own hearers: Acts 16:4; 1 Cor 11:2; 11:23 (first occurrence); 15:3; 2 Pet 2:21.
Teaching, custom or testimony is received from predecessors or an earlier generation: Mark 7:13; Luke 1:2; Acts 6:14; Jude 3.

Christ gives himself, or God gives his Son, on behalf of others, in an active construction with 'for us', 'for me' or 'for her': Rom 8:32; Gal 2:20; Eph 5:2; 5:25. The passive in Rom 4:25 and 1 Cor 11:23 stays 'hand over'.
Reflexive, of people surrendering themselves to vice: Eph 4:19. Where God is the subject in Rom 1:24, 26, 28 and Acts 7:42, keep 'hand over'.
Someone is committed to the care of God or God's grace: Acts 14:26; 15:40; 1 Pet 2:23.
With 'their lives' as object in Acts 15:26.
Intransitive, of a crop permitting harvest: Mark 4:29 only.

traditional: deliver or deliver up in general; betray when Judas is the subject; give up for Christ's self-giving; commit or commend for Acts 14:26 and 15:40
rationale: The verb is the ordinary Greek word for handing a person or thing into someone else's control. The Gospels use the same word for what Judas does, what the priests do to Jesus before Pilate, what Pilate does, and what will happen to the disciples. Greek has a separate word for betrayal, used of Judas in Luke 6:16. "Betray" names the treachery that the context supplies, but it hides that chain of handings-over, so one rendering lets the reader see what the Greek reader saw. The self-giving formulas keep the familiar "give up" because "hand himself over for me" is awkward English and adds no clarity.
standard_view: Most English versions (KJV, RSV, ESV, NIV, NRSV) render "betray" when Judas is the subject and "deliver", "hand over" or "give up" elsewhere. They usually say "arrested" or "put in prison" for John in Matt 4:12 and Mark 1:14, and "gave up his spirit" in John 19:30. The standard lexicons give "hand over, deliver up" as the basic sense. Many scholars hold that "betray" is a contextual inference and not the word's meaning, while others defend it as a legitimate contextual sense for Judas. The NABRE and several recent commentators use "hand over" more widely, as here.
